::: center
**Handout 24\
Confidence Intervals: Concepts**
:::

-   The estimators we have considered so far are *point* estimators; we
    estimate the population parameter $\theta$, an unknown number, by
    the observed sample statistic $\hat{\theta}$, a number which can be
    computed based on sample data.

-   For a particular sample a particular numerical value of
    $\hat{\theta}$ is observed, but there are many possible randomly
    selected samples and many possible values of the random variable
    $\hat{\theta}$.

-   While for any particular sample we hope the observed value of
    $\hat{\theta}$ is close to the true value of $\theta$, there will be
    some error in estimation due to natural sample-to-sample
    variability.

-   Because of this natural sample-to-sample variability, it is better
    to provide a range of values when estimating a parameter. This range
    of values is often (but not always) of the form: point estimate
    $\pm$ margin of error. The margin of error is chosen so that for
    "most" samples, the resulting interval will contain the true
    parameter value.

::: exer
**Exercise 1**. Suppose we wish to estimate the population mean $\mu$ of
a Normal distribution based on a sample of size $n$. For now, we'll
assume the population SD $\sigma$ is known. For example, suppose that
body temperatures (degrees F) of healthy adults follow a Normal
distribution with mean $\mu$ and SD $\sigma = 1.2$ degrees F. We wish to
estimate $\mu$ based on data from a sample of 208 healthy adults with
sample mean body temperature 97.7 degrees F[^1]. (Known population SD is
an unrealistic assumption. We will see how to handle unknown $\sigma$
later.)
:::

1.  Two choices for the plausible range for $\mu$ are
    $97.7\pm 3 \Rightarrow [94.7, 100.7]$ and
    $97.7\pm 0.001 \Rightarrow [97.699, 97.701]$. What are the
    advantages and disadvantages of each?

    **Solution:** The first interval is definitely correct; it's true
    *average* healthy adult body temp is somewhere between 94.7 and
    100.7 degrees F. But this interval is so imprecise that it doesn't
    give us any useful information.

    The second interval is much more precise. Saying average healthy
    adult body temp is between 97.699 and 97.701 is a much more
    informative conclusion. But is it correct? As an extreme, we could
    have said average body temperature of healthy adults *in general* is
    97.7 degrees F; a very precise statement but almost definitely
    wrong, because why should the sample mean match the population mean
    exactly? So there's a tradeoff between precision and accuracy.

    -   In determining a plausible range of values, there is a trade-off
        between

        -   Accuracy: does the true parameter value fall within the
            estimated range of values?

        -   Precision: the width of the range of estimated values

    -   The usual approach is to specify a desired degree of accuracy.
        Specifically, interval estimates are constructed so that they
        will be accurate "most of the time".

    -   A **confidence interval** estimates a population parameter based
        on sample data with

        -   a plausible range of values and

        -   a **confidence level** that the estimated range contains the
            true parameter value.

            -   By far, the most commonly used confidence level is 95%.
                (But see the material about multiple CIs at the end of
                this handout.)

    -   The endpoints of a confidence interval are usually given by
        $$\text{observed statistic} \pm \text{margin of error}$$

2.  What do you think will affect the margin of error? Consider the
    previous part. Also consider: what if the sample size had been 2080?
    Would the margin of error be larger or smaller? Why? How about if
    $\sigma$ were 0.6 degrees F?

    **Solution:** One thing is our level of confidence; a greater degree
    of confidence requires a wider interval and a larger margin of
    error.

    More importantly, the whole reason that we need an interval in the
    first is because samples exhibit natural sample-to-sample
    variability. If there is a lot of sample-to-sample variability ---
    e.g., if one sample gives a sample mean of 97.7 and another of 96.3
    and another of 98.9 --- then we need a wider interval. If there is
    little variability ---- e.g., if one sample gives a sample mean of
    97.7 and another of 97.9 and another of 97.6 --- then we can get
    away with a narrower and more precise interval.

    The main thing that impacts sample-to-sample variability of sample
    means is sample size. As the sample size increases, the
    sample-to-sample variability of sample means decreases. So the
    larger the sample size, the smaller the required margin of error for
    95% confidence, and the narrower and more precise the interval. The
    sample-to-sample variability of sample means is also influenced by
    the unit-to-unit population SD of individual value of the variables.

    The more body temperatures vary from person to person, the more
    sample means will vary from sample to sample, and the wider and less
    precise the interval required.

    -   The **margin of error** accounts for

        -   the confidence level (e.g. 95%),

            -   The larger the confidence level, the larger the margin
                of error --- and the wider the range of plausible values
                --- required to achieve that level of confidence.

        -   and the degree of sample-to-sample variability (SE) of the
            statistic.

            -   In general, the less variable the statistic (from sample
                to sample) the smaller the margin of error and the
                narrower the interval.

            -   In particular, the larger than sample size, the smaller
                the SE of the statistic, the smaller the margin of error
                and the narrower the interval.\

3.  Fill in the blank with both a general expression and the numerical
    value for this problem: for 95% of samples, the sample mean
    $\bar{X}$ is within \[blank\] of the population mean $\mu$.

    **Solution:** The sample-to-sample variability of $\bar{X}$ is
    $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 1.2/\sqrt{208} = 0.083$. Assuming $n$ is large
    enough so that $\bar{X}$ has a Normal distribution (which is true
    for any $n$ if the individual values are Normal), 95% of values of
    $\bar{X}$ are within $2\sigma/\sqrt{n}=2(0.083) = 0.166$ of $\mu$.
    (You might sometimes see 1.96 instead of 2; either is fine, 2 is
    simpler and conveys less of a false sense of precision.)

4.  Fill in $m$ with both a general expression and the numerical value
    for this problem: for 95% of samples, the interval with endpoints
    $\bar{X}\pm m$ will contain the population mean $\mu$.

    **Solution:** $2\sigma/\sqrt{n}=2(0.083) = 0.166$. This is just a
    restatement of the previous part. The samples where $\bar{X}$ is
    within $2\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ are the samples where the interval with
    endpoints $\bar{X}\pm  2\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ contains $\mu$.

5.  Use the procedure in the previous part to estimate $\mu$ based on
    the sample data ($n = 208$, $\bar{x}= 97.7$), and interpret your
    estimate.

    **Solution:** We're assuming $\sigma=1.2$ so with $n=208$ the margin
    of error for 95% confidence is
    $2\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 2(1.2)/\sqrt{208}=2(0.083)=0.166$. A 95%
    confidence interval for $\mu$ has endpoints
    $97.7\pm2(0.083)\Rightarrow 97.7\pm 0.166$ for an interval of
    $[97.5, 97.9]$. We estimate with 95% confidence that the population
    mean healthy human body temperature is between 97.5 and 97.9 deg F.

6.  Does the 95% confidence interval you computed in the previous part
    provide an accurate estimate of the corresponding parameter? That
    is, is $\mu$ contained within the CI? Explain.

    **Solution:** We don't know! We don't know what the true value of
    $\mu$ is; that's why we need to estimate it. We're "95% confident"
    that the interval contains the true value of $\mu$, but we don't
    know for sure. We could be wrong.

    Another issue is potential bias in data collection. Confidence
    intervals only account for sample-to-sample variability, but what
    about bias in data collection? We need to ask: How were the data
    collected? See the part about generalizing below.

    -   Because the value of the parameter is *unknown*, we never know
        for sure whether any one confidence interval contains the
        parameter or not.

    -   But the procedure guarantees that in the long run --- that is,
        over many unbiased random samples --- "most" confidence
        intervals will contain the parameter, regardless of what the
        true value of the parameter is. "Most" is determined by the
        level of confidence.\

7.  Could you reasonably conclude that population mean human body
    temperature is less than 98.6 degrees F? Why?

    **Solution:** The confidence interval lies entirely below the value
    98.6. So yes, we can conclude with 95% confidence that population
    mean body temp is less than 98.6 degrees F. But we could be wrong.
    We're confident that we're right, but we'll never know for sure.
    (There's lots of evidence that 98.6 is a very outdated number that
    unfortunately persists; see the article links in the above
    footnote.)

    -   Any value within the confidence interval is a plausible value of
        the parameter

    -   Values outside of the confidence interval are not plausible
        values of the parameter

    -   The CI could be wrong; we are confident that it is correct, but
        we'll never know for sure\

8.  To what extent can you generalize your results? What are some issues
    to consider?

    **Solution:** We need to ask: How were the data collected? Assuming
    it's a reasonably representative sample of healthy humans with
    respect to body temperatures, there should be minimial bias. The
    main thing to check would be to see where the temperatures were
    collected to verify if the people could be reasonably considered
    healthy. (If they were all taken during visits to the doctor, then
    maybe some of the people where sick.)

    When investigating bias, the crucial issue is who are the units in
    the sample and how were they selected, rather than how many. Sample
    size mainly affects sample-to-sample variability, and our margin of
    error accounts for that.

    -   There are two sources of differences between a statistic and a
        corresponding parameter

        -   systematic errors due to **bias**

        -   "chance errors" due to **sampling variability**

    -   While there is no bias inherent in simple random sampling from a
        population, bias can be present in other ways, including
        undercoverage, nonresponse, wording of questions, etc.

    -   Bias concerns the *center* of the sampling distribution of a
        statistic. A biased sampling procedure produces values which
        consistently overestimate or consistently underestimate the
        respective parameter.

    -   The inference procedures --- confidence intervals and hypothesis
        tests --- we will encounter assume that the data are collected
        in an unbiased way from a random sample.

    -   If there is bias present in data collection then the observed
        statistic (i.e. the center of the confidence interval) is likely
        to be a poor estimate of the parameter.

    -   The margin of error in a confidence interval only accounts for
        sampling variability, NOT bias.

    -   To see if bias is present --- in which case the confidence
        interval cannot be trusted --- ask: how were the data
        collected?\

9.  What if we wanted 95% confidence, but we wanted the margin of error
    to be no bigger than 0.01. How could we achieve this?

    **Solution:** Increase the sample size! Though this is sometimes
    easier said than done. Collecting body temperatures for healthy
    people is fairly easy. But in many situations there are many
    obstacles to collecting more data: time, money, ethical
    considerations, etc. (For example, testing on humans an experimental
    vaccine for which the side effects are unknown.)

-   A $1-\alpha$ **confidence interval** for $\theta$ is an *interval
    estimator* of $\theta$ of the form\
    $[L(X_1,\ldots,X_n), U(X_1,\ldots,X_n)]$ which satisfies
    $$\textrm{P}_\theta\left(L(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\le \theta\le U(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\right) = 1-\alpha$$

-   $L(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $U(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ represent, respectively,
    the lower and upper endpoints of the interval. $L$ and $U$ are
    *random variables* that vary from sample-to-sample.

-   Typical values of $\alpha$ include 0.05 and 0.01. We express
    $1-\alpha$ as a percentage. For example, $\alpha=0.05$ corresponds
    to a 95% confidence interval.

-   A confidence interval estimates a population parameter based on
    sample data with

    -   a plausible range of values and

    -   a confidence level that the estimated range contains the true
        parameter value.

-   Often $L=\hat{\theta}-M$ and $U=\hat{\theta}+M$, where the **margin
    of error** $M$ --- where $M$ can be a RV --- accounts for both the
    sample-to-sample variability of $\hat{\theta}$ and the confidence
    level.

-   The margin of error is often of the form: multiple of standard error

-   The multiple is determined by the confidence level and the
    distribution of the point estimator $\hat{\theta}$ (e.g., 2 for 95%
    confidence when the estimator follows a Normal distribution.)

-   The **standard error** is the estimated sample-to-sample SD of the
    estimator,
    $\textrm{SE}(\hat{\theta})= \widehat{\textrm{SD}}(\hat{\theta})$.

-   Many confidence intervals take the form
    $$\text{statistic} \pm \text{multiple of its SE}$$

-   The multiple (a.k.a. **critical value**) depends on the confidence
    level and the shape of the sample-to-sample distribution of the
    statistic over many samples.

-   For many statistics (e.g. proportions, means, differences in means)
    the sample-to-sample variation of values of the statistic over many
    unbiased random samples has an approximate Normal shape centered at
    the true value of the population parameter

-   When the pattern of variation of the sample statistic can be
    reasonably approximated by a Normal distribution, the multiple is
    usually denoted $z^*$; common values include:\

    ::: center
      ------------------------------- ----- ----- ----- ------- --------
      Confidence level ($1-\alpha$)     90%   95%   99%   99.7%   99.99%
      Critical value ($z^*$)            1.7   2.0   2.6     3.0      4.0
                                                                
      ------------------------------- ----- ----- ----- ------- --------
    :::

    where $z^*$ is the critical value from the standard normal
    distribution corresponding to level $1-\alpha$\

::: exer
**Exercise 2**. For each of the following statements, identify if it is
a valid interpretation of the CI from the previous exercise. If not,
explain why.
:::

1.  We estimate that 95% of the people in the population have body
    temperatures between 97.5 and 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Not valid. Interval is about the mean, not individual
    body temps.

2.  We estimate with 95% confidence that the sample mean body
    temperature is between 97.5 and 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Not valid. Interval is about the population mean; we
    know what the sample mean is.

3.  We estimate with 95% confidence that the population mean healthy
    human body temperature is between 97.5 and 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Valid.

4.  If many samples of size 208 were selected about 95% would produce a
    CI of 97.5 to 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Not valid. The sample means and resulting intervals
    will from sample to sample.

5.  In about 95% of samples of size 208, the sample mean body
    temperature will be between 97.5 and 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Not valid. Not making statements about the sample
    mean.

6.  In about 95% of samples of size 208, the population mean body
    temperature will be between 97.5 and 97.9 degrees F.\

    **Solution:** Not valid. $\mu$ is a number; it's either between 97.5
    and 97.9 or not.

7.  If many hypothetical unbiased random samples of size 208 were
    selected, and a 95% confidence interval computed based on each
    sample, about 95% of these confidence intervals would contain the
    population mean body temperature.\

    **Solution:** Valid. This is what "95% confidence" means.

-   A CI is a conclusion about a population parameter --- a number that
    *summarizes* the population (e.g. the population mean) --- and not
    about individual values of a variable.

-   The conclusions from inference regard the *population* from which
    the random sample was selected; there is nothing to conclude for the
    sample.

-   No one particular sample (e.g. the one observed) or CI is
    necessarily good or representative of the many other possible
    samples or CIs.

-   The randomness is in the *sampling procedure*, which determines $L$
    and $U$, and not the parameter. The parameter $\theta$ is a fixed
    number. After selecting the sample, there is no randomness left.
    Either the CI contains the parameter or not; you just don't know
    which it is.

-   We are confident in our observed estimate because we are confident
    in our estimation *procedure*

    -   By considering what would happen over many hypothetical random
        samples we are able to determine the necessary margin of error
        so that our CIs would contain the parameter in 95% of samples.

    -   Because the value of the parameter is unknown, we never know for
        sure whether any one confidence interval contains the parameter
        or not.

    -   But the procedure guarantees that in the long run --- that is,
        over many unbiased random samples --- "most" confidence
        intervals will contain the parameter, regardless of what the
        true value of the parameter is. "Most" is determined by the
        level of confidence.

::: exer
**Exercise 3**. Suppose we wish to estimate population mean GPA of
students at each of the 23 CSU campuses. For each campus, you select a
random sample of students, collect the GPAs of the students, and then
use the sample data to compute a 95% confidence interval. That is you
compute 23 separate 95% confidence intervals, one for the population
mean GPA at each campus.
:::

1.  First just consider Cal Poly. What is the probability that your
    confidence interval based on the Cal Poly sample contains the true
    population mean GPA at Cal Poly?

    **Solution:** 0.95. 95% confidence means that for 95% of samples the
    CI will contain the true parameter value. So the probability that we
    get one of the "good" samples with a "good" interval is 0.95.

2.  What is the probability that all 23 of your 95% confidence intervals
    contain their respective population mean?

    **Solution:** The probability that any single interval contains its
    parameter is 0.95. The samples are selected independently, so the
    probability that all 23 contain their respective parameters is
    $0.95^{23} = 0.307$

3.  How confident are you that all 23 of your 95% confidence intervals
    contain their respective population mean?

    **Solution:** Even though each interval is a 95% confidence
    interval, we're only 30% confident that all the intervals contain
    their respective parameters. Over many sets of 23 samples with 23
    intervals, all the CIs contains their parameters in only 30% of
    sets.

    -   When computing multiple confidence intervals, the multiple
        ($z^*$ or $t^*$) of each confidence interval should be increased
        to account for the **issue of multiple comparisons**.

        -   For example, with a multiple of 2 in a *single* confidence
            interval, we are 95% confident that the interval contains
            the corresponding parameter.

        -   However, if we use a multiple of 2 for each of 10 confidence
            intervals, we are only 60% confident[^2] that *all* of the
            10 95% confidence intervals contain their respective
            parameters.

    -   A **Bonferroni** adjustment, splits the error rate evenly across
        all intervals. For example, for simultaneous 95% confidence in
        10 intervals (i.e. a total error rate of 0.05), use the
        $z^*/t^*$ multiple for 99.5% confidence when constructing each
        interval.

        -   A Bonferroni adjustment guarantees **simultaneous
            confidence**

        -   But it is conservative, and tends to produce wider intervals
            than necessary

        -   There are other methods; for example, the *Tukey-Kramer
            method* is often used for *all pairwise comparisons of
            means* (e.g., in ANOVA)\

4.  Suppose we want simultaneous 95% confidence that all 23 CIs contain
    their respective mean. Find the $z^*$ multiple corresponding to a
    Bonferroni adjustment. How many times wider will each CI be than the
    unadjusted intervals?

    **Solution:** The total error rate is 0.05, split over 23 intervals
    gives 0.0022 for each, so we use the $z^*$ multiple for 99.78%
    confidence. That is, we need to find the value $z^*$ which
    satisfies: For a Normal distribution, 99.78% of values are within
    $z^*$ SDs of the mean, so 0.11% in either tail. Using software
    `qnorm(1 - 0.0011)` = 3.07.

    Compared to the multiple of 2 for individual 95% confidence, each
    interval is now 3.07/2 = 1.53 times wider, or about 53% wider.

5.  How confident are you that all 23 of your adjusted confidence
    intervals contain their respective population mean?

    **Solution:** The probability that any single interval contains its
    parameter is now 0.9978. The samples are selected independently, so
    the probability that all 23 contain their respective parameters is
    $0.9978^{23} = 0.951$. So we are simultaneously 95% confident that
    all 23 of the CIs contain their respective population mean.

[^1]: Source: <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6258625/>
    and a [related
    article](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-human-body-temperatures-cooling-down/).

[^2]: This number assumes independence of confidence intervals ---
    $0.95^{10}\approx 0.60$ --- but similar ideas apply more generally.
